title: Stream fragment recovery and client liveness policy
creator: Aisha Khan
description:
Problem: When clients disconnect mid-generation (abrupt TCP close, browser tab close, or API timeout), we accumulate partial generation state (KV cache entries, in-flight batch slots, and buffered tokens). Current heuristics sometimes leave fragments uncollected, causing wasted GPU work, incorrect token accounting, and noisy logs.

Goal: Define a deterministic, low-cost protocol and server-side lifecycle for recoverable stream fragments and client liveness that: 1) minimizes wasted work and cost, 2) provides clean accounting for partial responses, 3) enables compatibility with existing HTTP streaming and websocket modes, and 4) preserves semantic guarantees for function/tool calls and structured outputs.

Scope: runtime serving layer, API gateway, and SDK compatibility layer. Workitems: explicit liveness signals, server-side fragment checkpoints, GC policy for orphaned fragments, client best-practice guidance, observability and SLOs, migration plan for older clients.

Proposed approach/decisions: 
- Connection liveness: define two complementary signals: (a) transport-level: user-initiated FIN/GOAWAY handling (HTTP/1.1 chunked, HTTP/2 stream close, websockets close), and (b) application-level heartbeats: optional X-Client-Liveness ping (SSE/HTTP streaming) or a WebSocket PING message. Default retention TTL = 20s after transport close unless explicit Resume-Token provided.
- Fragment checkpointing: for long-running generations (>500ms server compute), emit periodic fragment checkpoints (opaque resume tokens) containing minimal metadata: model version, seed, KV-cache pointers, prefix-length, and byte-offset. Tokens are HMACed and short-lived (TTL=5m).
- Resume semantics: clients can resume using a Resume-Token within TTL; server will attempt to reconcile prefix/KV cache and continue generation without re-running full prefix computation. Resume falls back to safe re-generation when mismatch or token expired.
- Partial output accounting: when transport closes before completion, record a PartialGeneration event with reason code (CLIENT_DISCONNECT | TIMEOUT | SERVER_SHUTDOWN | BACKPRESSURE_DROP) and token_count produced. Billing signals will use guarded rounding rules to avoid double-billing on resume.
- Backpressure policy: expose X-Flow-Window header on responses indicating allowed outstanding tokens for the connection. SDKs should use it to adapt client-side concurrency. Server will also apply per-client token-budget and reject aggressive reopen attempts with 429 + Retry-After.
- Garbage collection: orphaned fragment garbage collection runs tiered: (1) soft GC at 20s (evict ephemeral buffers, allow resume if token present), (2) hard GC at 5m (release KV cache slots and GPUs). Admins can configure shorter retention for Dedicated customers.
- Compatibility layer: implement server-side bridges for legacy clients that do not support resume tokens: provide a best-effort fast-restart path that uses cached prefix hashes; annotate responses with structured diagnostics to indicate whether resume is supported.

Open trade-offs: 
- Tokenized resume vs. full checkpoint size: smaller tokens leak less info and are cheaper, but increase the chance of re-generation. We choose minimal metadata and rely on HMAC verification.
- TTL values: conservatively chosen to balance cost and UX; Dedicated customers may require configurable TTLs.
- Backpressure semantics across protocols: HTTP chunked/SSE lacks native windowing; we add headers and SDK conventions instead of changing transport.

Acceptance criteria: 
- Unit and integration tests for resume token lifecycle and mismatch handling.
- E2E test: client disconnect -> resume within TTL -> resulting generation matches baseline within tolerance (same final structured output when deterministic seed used).
- Metrics: count of PartialGeneration events, wasted GPU-seconds from orphaned fragments reduced by >=70% in canary region.
- Billing: ensure no double-billing on resume path.
- Docs/SDK: document SDK helpers to surface Resume-Token and X-Flow-Window handling.

Migration/rollout plan: 
1) Implement server-side fragment checkpoints and GC but keep resume disabled (emit tokens for telemetry).
2) Rollout small canary (5% of traffic) enabling resume for internal customers.
3) Expand to 25%, run observability checks (PartialGeneration rate, GPU waste).
4) Enable by default and publish SDK updates and quickstart guidance.

comments: 2025-01-16 - Miguel Torres: Spiked a prototype for resume tokens. The HMAC design works, but we need to ensure KV cache pointers are compacted. Logged perf numbers in the PR.

2025-01-20 - Priya Nair (PM): Important to scope the UX for function-calls where partial outputs could trigger side effects. We should gate resume for streams that produced tool/invoke events unless the client opted in.
2025-01-25 - Devlin Park (Design): Suggest adding a small visual indicator in Console that a response was resumed and that some tokens were from checkpointed continuation. Helps SRE/debugging.
2025-01-28 - Security review (meta): Resume tokens HMACed; threat model approved, but recommended rotating signing keys monthly. See notes in Confluence.
2025-01-31 - QA: Added tests to simulate connection flaps and TTL expiry. Found a race where partial billing event fired twice; added a de-dup marker to PartialGeneration entries.
2025-02-02 - Miguel Torres: Implemented soft GC and Resume-Token generation. Ready for internal canary. Created canary job and dashboard: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/stream-recovery-canary
